opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions in the field right now. Language models give us an incredible prior about the world: they know that cups hold liquid, that you open a drawer before putting something in it, that a kitchen task has some reasonable ordering of steps. That kind of semantic, common-sense knowledge used to be really hard to get into a robot, and now we get a lot of it almost for free. So I don't want to downplay it at all.

But when you look at where robots actually fail, it's rarely because the robot didn't know *what* to do. It's because it didn't know *how* to do it physically. Think about inserting a plug into a socket, folding a shirt, or using a tool where the contact forces really matter. The hard part lives in the continuous, high-frequency interaction between the robot's body and the world: friction, compliance, small misalignments, objects deforming in ways you didn't expect. None of that is well represented in text. Nobody writes on the internet, "apply about two newtons more force and rotate three degrees while you feel the edge catch." That knowledge is mostly tacit. Humans have it in their hands, not in their words.

So language priors help you a lot at the level of task planning and abstraction, but the bottleneck in robotics is grounding: connecting those abstractions to perception and to low-level control in a closed loop. That's also why the data problem in robotics is so different. For language models, the internet was this huge pre-existing dataset. For physical interaction, there is no equivalent sitting around. We have to collect it, whether through teleoperation, simulation, or, as I'm quite excited about, learning from humans doing things naturally, and then figure out how to transfer that to robot embodiments.

There's also a reliability issue. In language, if the model is right ninety percent of the time, that's often useful. In the physical world, a ten percent failure rate can mean broken objects or someone getting hurt, and errors compound over long horizons. You need the system to notice when things go wrong and recover, and that requires a real understanding of physical state, not just a plausible-sounding plan.

So my view is that language models are a powerful ingredient, but the hardest problems in robotics, dexterity, contact-rich manipulation, long-horizon robustness, generalizing across bodies and environments, require priors about physics and embodiment that we have to build from physical experience. That's where a lot of the interesting research is going to be over the next several years.

r001.rationale: It contrasts language models’ semantic and task-level knowledge with robotics’ difficult physical interactions, including contact forces, friction, compliance, and tacit skills absent from text.

r002.rationale: It says language priors help with task planning and abstraction, while fine, contact-rich manipulation and low-level control are the robotics bottleneck.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, I want to be careful here, because I actually think language models have been incredibly useful for robotics. They've given us a way to do high-level task decomposition, to ground instructions, to get a kind of common-sense scaffolding that we just didn't have five or six years ago. So I'm not anti-LLM at all.

But when I think about what the genuinely hard problems in robotics are, they tend to live in a layer that language was never designed to describe. Language is a lossy compression of the world that humans built for talking to other humans. It carries the things we found worth saying. It mostly doesn't carry the things we never had to say, because our bodies already knew them. Nobody writes down how much force to apply when you're sliding a key into a slightly sticky lock, or how a towel folds differently depending on how damp it is, or how a stack of dishes starts to wobble right before it tips. There's basically no text on the internet about that, because no human ever needed to read it.

So when we take a language-model prior and push it down into low-level manipulation, we hit this wall. The model can tell you "pick up the cup and put it on the shelf," and that's great, that's planning. But the actual problem, the thing that makes the robot fail in your kitchen, is that the cup is half full, the handle is at a weird angle, there's a fork in the way, and the shelf is slightly too high. All of those details are in the physics and the perception, in continuous contact dynamics, and language has almost nothing to say about them.

The other thing I'd point to is that language-model knowledge is essentially static. It reflects what was written down, not what happens when you act and the world pushes back. Robotics is fundamentally an interactive, closed-loop problem. You take an action, something unexpected happens, and you have to adapt in real time. A prior that's never had to deal with consequences is going to be miscalibrated about what's easy and what's hard in the physical world. LLMs are confidently wrong about physical feasibility all the time. They'll propose plans that look totally reasonable in text and are completely impossible for the actual embodiment.

And then there's the embodiment question itself. A language model doesn't know what body it's in. Whether you have a two-finger gripper or a dexterous hand, whether your arm has a reach of 60 centimeters or a meter, that changes what counts as a good plan. Language gives you an abstract, body-agnostic view of the world, and robots are anything but body-agnostic.

So my view is that language priors are a fantastic top layer, but the hardest problems are in the middle and the bottom. The middle being how do you bridge from a symbolic plan to a sequence of motions that actually respect the geometry and dynamics of the scene. The bottom being how do you learn robust, contact-rich, closed-loop skills from the kind of data a robot can realistically collect. I think solving those needs priors that come from interaction, from large-scale robot and human motion data, from simulation, from learning models of how the world responds. Language can orchestrate that. It can't substitute for it.

So I'd say language got us surprisingly far, surprisingly fast, and that's exactly why it's tempting to think it'll get us the rest of the way. I just don't think the remaining distance is a language problem.

r001.rationale: The response says language priors lack the physical, interactive, and embodiment-specific knowledge needed for robotics’ hardest problems.

r002.rationale: It contrasts language models’ useful high-level task planning with the harder low-level manipulation challenges involving contact, physics, and real-time adaptation.

astra-6.text:
I think language models give us a powerful prior about what might make sense to do. But in robotics, knowing what to do at a high level is different from knowing how to make it happen in the physical world.

Take something as simple as plugging in a cable. A language model can tell you to align the connector and push it in. The hard part is sensing whether it’s actually aligned, how much force to apply, and what to change when it gets stuck. Those decisions depend on contact, geometry, and feedback that aren’t fully captured in a language description.

So the limitation isn’t that language is unhelpful. It’s that a prior has to be grounded in interaction. The robot needs to act, observe the consequences, and correct its behavior. For the hardest problems, that ability to learn from physical experience and respond to what’s happening is essential. Language can help guide the process, but it doesn’t supply that capability by itself.

r001.rationale: It contrasts language models’ high-level guidance with robotics challenges that require sensing contact and geometry, applying force, and adapting through physical feedback.

r002.rationale: It says knowing what to do at a high level is different from making it happen physically, then identifies fine manipulation details as the hard part.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language models give us a very useful prior about what might work, but that’s different from knowing what will work in the physical world. You can describe how to pick up an object, but the description doesn’t tell you exactly where to make contact, how much force to apply, or how to react when it starts slipping. Those details depend on the robot, the object, and the state of the environment at that moment.

The hardest robotics problems often live in that gap. A plan can sound completely reasonable and still fail when you execute it. So the robot needs experience and feedback: it needs to act, observe the consequences, and adjust. Language can help guide that process, but it doesn’t replace learning from physical interaction.

r001.rationale: It contrasts language models’ useful general priors with the physical-world details and feedback that make difficult robotics tasks challenging.

r002.rationale: It says a reasonable-sounding plan may fail in execution and gives manipulation examples, but does not state that task planning is much easier than fine manipulation.
